text.approach: Reached via a multi-day backpack up the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground to Park Creek Pass (roughly 40 miles round trip with on the order of 7,000 ft of cumulative gain including the bonus climb to Junction Camp), or as part of a Ptarmigan-style traverse linking Cascade Pass/Buckner/Park Creek Pass. From a Park Creek Pass-area camp, it is a short day-trip scramble up to the Booker-Buckner col and on to the summit.

text.overview: An alternate Class 3 scramble reached from Park Creek Pass via the Booker-Buckner col, on the mountain's northwest side; used mainly by parties already in the Park Creek/Buckner area on a multi-day traverse rather than as a dedicated approach.
text.descent: Downclimb the northwest-side Class 3 terrain back to the Booker-Buckner col, then descend the broad sandy gully (using snowbridges over any crevasses/cracks as on the ascent) back toward Park Creek Pass camp.

text.approach: Reached via the Chain Lakes/Doelle Lakes basin as part of a multi-day traverse (e.g. the 'Bullseye Traverse'), continuing cross-country south to Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft) before dropping packs and climbing the south side of the peak. No standalone trailhead-to-base mileage for this specific line is documented; it is climbed as a side trip from a traverse camp.
text.road: {"name":"Same access as Standard Scramble (Stevens Pass/PCT or Icicle Creek Road)","status":null,"driveNote":null,"seasonalGate":null}
text.overview: A harder, more direct line up Bulls Tooth's south ridge from Bullseye Pass, done by parties on the multi-summit 'Bullseye Traverse'; unlike the standard notch scramble, this line finishes with a short, roped Class 4-5 pitch to the true summit.
text.descent: From the summit, three rappels on a ~40m rope are needed to get back down through the technical section to easier ground; the granite here is compact with few holds and was reported as harder to reverse than to climb — one party found a heather-camouflaged hole in the rock during the down-climb. Below the rappels, reverse the Class 3 traverse back around the peak to Bullseye Pass.

text.overview: The lower part is roughly 8-10 pitches, none above 5.6, finishing in a couloir of 400ft that steepens to 50 degrees when snow-covered. Four more pitches, as hard as 5.8, reach the top. Come down the North Face.

text.approach: Start from the end of Forest Service road 4096 and follow the Bedal Creek trail, which is rough and blown down in places. Where the tread is lost in a rocky creek bed, keep going up the creek through one short wet step until the path reappears on the right. The trail fades in the heather beneath the southwest face of Sloan; from the basin there, climb about a thousand feet south to the ridge crest. Drop on grassy, rocky ground to the small tarn often called Cadet Lake, cross over Heineken Peak, and go down its steep grassy gullies to a low point near 5,600 ft above the remnant Mayflower Glacier. The route starts there, on the ridge rising on the northeast side of Cadet Peak toward a small hanging glacier.
text.overview: A high alpine ridge traverse linking Sloan Peak to Cadet Peak's northeast ridge and face, following the timberline crest between the two mountains rather than a direct up-and-down approach to Cadet alone.
text.descent: Cross the summit plateau and come down the standard route toward Glacier Basin. The upper cliff band is the tricky part when you did not climb the standard line: follow cairns and look for the worn boot path through it. Lower down a tunnel through the brush leads into Glacier Basin. The whole descent is steep and loose, hard on the knees, but not technical. From the basin pick up the Glacier Basin

text.approach: Identical to Rebel Yell. Drive SR 20 to Washington Pass, then about 4 miles east to a wide pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166, at roughly 4,250 ft (about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road, about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn). No Northwest Forest Pass is required on the highway shoulder. Descend a steep, faint scree path about 300 ft to Early Winters Creek, cross on logs, then follow the climbers' trail steeply uphill to a wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft - the standard low camp, with a year-round spring about 200 yards north of the trail and a seasonal spring in the sandy gully above. Above the bench the trail fades; follow cairns up loose gullies, trending right and up, into the main gully below Burgundy Col at 7,800-7,950 ft. The gully holds a roughly 40-degree snow finger into midsummer. Roughly 3.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to the col in 3-4 hours. From the col, descend 200-300 ft on the south side and traverse right beneath Burgundy Spire's east face on year-round snow with seasonal rock bands until Chianti's east face is in view. Rebel Yell's dihedral is the obvious feature on the right side of the face; Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. Under an hour from the col.

text.overview: The original 1952 first-ascent line up Chianti Spire, gained by rappelling into the Burgundy-Chianti notch and climbing the peak's north side on then-loose rock; now rarely repeated in favor of the East Face/Rebel Yell.
text.descent: Downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block back onto the north face, then reverse the line to the Burgundy-Chianti notch. From the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy Spire's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col - this re-ascent is the sting in the tail and is much easier on firm morning snow than on afternoon slush or bare, sandy rock. text.approach: From US 101 about 36 miles north of Hoquiam (one mile south of Amanda Park), turn east on the Lake Quinault South Shore Road and follow it toward the head of the valley; the first ~10 miles are paved and the remainder is gravel, ending after roughly 20 miles at the Graves Creek Trailhead (47.57255, -123.56997, 550 ft). Note the detour: South Shore Road has been closed by a washout about 8 miles from US 101, with Graves Creek Road reachable via the North Shore Road instead — check park road conditions or the road hotline at 360-565-3131 before you drive, and note that RVs and trailers are prohibited on Graves Creek Road. From the trailhead, follow the East Fork Quinault River (Enchanted Valley) Trail up the rainforest valley. It is 27.8 miles round trip and about 3,700 ft of gain to Enchanted Valley, so roughly 13.9 miles and a high point near 2,035 ft one way; the Enchanted Valley Chalet (47.67528, -123.38917) sits at about 2,000 ft directly beneath the peak's south wall. Chimney Peak's south side above the valley is a 4,800 ft wall of cliffs and waterfalls and is not the way up — the climbing approach leaves the trail and works around to the peak's southwest side to gain the Southwest Ridge, then traverses to the base of The Chimney on the west aspect. Expect to find your own way on the off-trail section.

text.overview: A short but distinct technical line up the 100-ft rock tower on Chimney Peak's west side that gives the mountain its name — a separate, harder objective from the peak's class 3 SW-ridge summit scramble.
text.descent: There is no published descent beta for this tower. In practice you reverse your line: get off the 100 ft tower, regain the class 3 ground on the Southwest Ridge and downclimb it, then retrace the off-trail approach back down to the East Fork Quinault trail and Enchanted Valley. waypoints.name: Graves Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From US 101 about 36 miles north of Hoquiam, one mile south of Amanda Park, turn east onto the Lake Quinault South Shore Road and follow it toward the head of the valley. The first 10 miles or so are paved and the rest is gravel, ending after roughly 20 miles at the Graves Creek Trailhead at 550 ft; allow about an hour for that final 20 miles. South Shore Road has been closed by a washout about 8 miles in, with Graves Creek Road reachable via the North Shore Road instead, so check park road conditions or the road hotline at 360-565-3131 before you drive. RVs and trailers are prohibited on Graves Creek Road.

waypoints.name: Enchanted Valley Chalet (emergency shelter and camp area beneath the peak)
waypoints.directions: Follow the East Fork Quinault River Trail from Graves Creek, along an old roadbed for the first 2 miles and then down to cross the river on Pony Bridge at about 2.5 miles. Continue up the rainforest valley on a gentle grade past O'Neil Creek, No Name Creek and Pyrites Creek camps, then cross the river again on a high bridge to reach the meadows of Enchanted Valley and the chalet at about 2,000 ft, nearly 14 miles from the trailhead.

text.approach: This route shares the same trailhead-to-basin approach as the East Face: from the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616, hike the Pete Lake Trail #1323 (~4 easy miles to Pete Lake, then ~2 more miles) to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, head north on the PCT about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche-path crossing, then leave the PCT and follow the climber's path (flagged/cairned, fords Chimney Creek and crosses several brushy ravines) up through Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft, ~4-5 hrs from the trailhead) to the moraine and the bivy basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier (~5,400 ft) — see the East Face route's approach text for full turn-by-turn detail on this shared stretch, and treat it as a 2-3 day car-to-car trip. Above camp, a wet, grubby gully through the rock band leads onto the upper Chimney Glacier; rope up, cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, and be ready to improvise around the moat at the foot of the rock, which gets worse later in the season. Water and camping options match the East Face approach: Pete Lake, the low Chimney Creek crossings, or melted glacier snow above the moraine.

text.overview: Chimney Rock is a steep peak on the Cascade Crest in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness with three summits: the central spire (7,727 ft) is the highest, the north peak is 7,634 ft, and the minor south peak is 7,440 ft. This line climbs the south peak. From the Chimney Glacier it takes wet fourth-class ground and ledges up the east side to the notch between the central and south summits, then continues about 400 ft to the top.
text.descent: Descend the line of ascent. From the South Peak, return about 400 ft to the notch between the central and south summits, then follow the ledge system back down; the ledges are easy to pick out from above. Rappel the steeper, wet fourth-class steps on a single 60 m rope rather than downclimbing them. No fixed anchors are known on this line, so carry slings, cord and a few rap rings to build and lea

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass honored in the lot; fill out the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Reached on FR-4616 off Cooper Lake Road, past Cooper Lake.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established shoreline campsites on the north side; the last easy water before the PCT junction.
waypoints.directions: Roughly four miles of easy, nearly flat forest trail. The tread is in good shape and gets dusty by midsummer, and it is walked fast — none of the day's real work is here.

waypoints.name: PCT Junction near Lemah Meadows
waypoints.note: Pete Lake Trail meets the PCT here; turn north toward Lemah Meadows rather than continuing to Spectacle Lake.
waypoints.directions: Carry on past the lake on the Pete Lake Trail to where it meets the PCT — a short, gentle stretch. Fill up before leaving the lake; above here water means Chimney Creek or melted snow.

waypoints.name: Climber's trail, east side of Chimney Creek
waypoints.note: A climber's path, marked with orange flagging in places, follows the east bank of Chimney Creek up toward Sunrise Knob, staying above the avalanche debris used by the East Face approach.
waypoints.directions: Head north on the PCT about a mile to where it crosses the Chimney Creek avalanche path, and leave the trail there. A logjam gives the creek crossing, and the climber's path starts faint on the far side, running about twenty yards inside the forest alongside the avalanche slope before it firms up. Losing the start puts you in the brush of the avalanche path itself, which is what the flagging is there to prevent.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Knob
waypoints.note: Shared basecamp for both Chimney Rock routes, on a knob just below the moraine overlooking the falls.
waypoints.directions: Steep, brushy climbing up the east bank, crossing several ravines, to the rock buttress at the top. Budget four to five hours from the car to here — the mileage is modest but nearly all the gain and all the route-finding sit in this last stretch.

waypoints.name: Chimney Glacier / moat crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the moat where the upper Chimney Glacier meets the rock; it widens through the season, so look for collapsed snow blocks or a bridge where it narrows.
waypoints.directions: Climb the moraine above camp; a wet, grubby gully through the rock band is the usual way onto the ice, avoiding the icefall. Rope up and cross the upper glacier toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, keeping clear of the deep bergschrund.

waypoints.name: Notch between the summits
waypoints.note: Roughly three pitches (~600 vertical ft) of wet, slippery ledges and cracks gain this notch between the central and south summits; also used as a rappel/downclimb station on descent.
waypoints.directions: Climb the face to the left of the main gully: about three pitches of wet, slippery fourth-class ground, then a system of ledges, some very wide, to just below the notch. Everything here stays wet, so the short fourth-class steps feel harder than their grade.

waypoints.name: Chimney Rock, South Summit
waypoints.note: South Peak, about 400 vertical feet above the notch; descend by downclimbing the ascent ledges and rappelling the steeper steps.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, continue about 400 ft to the top of the South Peak. This is Chimney Rock's lower south summit, not the central main summit (7,727 ft) that the East Face route climbs. Come down the same way: the ledges are easy to pick out from above, and the steeper sections go with single-rope rappels.

name: The Foot of Faith - West Face P3 variation

text.overview: Follows the vegetated corner until an overlap, above which the 1984 Variation drifts slightly left. This one traverses right on a few good edges until they fade, then relies on a smear to reach an arete. A crux fall is perhaps PG-13, swinging back into the corner. Follow the arete, traverse right along a horizontal break and join the big ledge at the end of pitch 3. Alternatively link into the 5.8 alternate start of pitch 4, belaying beneath the enduro corner.

Alternative to the third pitch. Where climbers normally step rightward on to the pillar after roughly 20 ft, this goes directly up into a lightly vegetated, left-facing corner, passing a block wrapped in purple slings (in 2025) that offers an optional belay or a way to retreat to the pillar. Believed to be a 5.8 corner with flaring walls, then a layback or squeeze at 5.9+; the upper part is uncertain.
